Jesus Entering on His Public Ministry, Makes a Circuit of Galilee--Rejection at Nazareth.</title> <div sID="gen27755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Note.--</hi>A large gap here occurs, embracing the important transactions in Galilee and Jerusalem which are recorded in Joh 1:29-4:54, and which occurred before John's imprisonment (<reference osisRef="John.3.24">Joh 3:24</reference>); whereas the transactions here recorded occurred (as appears from <reference osisRef="Matt.4.12">Mt 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.13">13</reference>) after that event. The visit to Nazareth recorded in <reference osisRef="Matt.13.54-Matt.13.58">Mt 13:54-58</reference> (and <reference osisRef="Mark.6.1-Mark.6.6">Mr 6:1-6</reference>) we take to be not a later visit, but the same with this first one; because we cannot think that the Nazarenes, after being so enraged at His first display of wisdom as to attempt His destruction, should, on a second display of the same, wonder at it and ask how He came by it, as if they had never witnessed it before.<div eID="gen27755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14324"/><hi type="bold">16. as his custom was--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.17.2">Ac 17:2</reference>.<div eID="gen27756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stood up for to read--</hi>Others besides rabbins were allowed to address the congregation. entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 4 Lu 4:1-13 . Temptation of Christ. (See on Mt 4:1-11 .) Lu 4:14-32 . Jesus Entering on His Public Ministry, Makes a Circuit of Galilee--Rejection at Nazareth. Note.-- A large gap here occurs, embracing the important transactions in Galilee and Jerusalem which are recorded in Joh 1:29-4:54, and which occurred before John's imprisonment ( Joh 3:24 ); whereas the transactions here recorded occurred (as appears from Mt 4:12 , 13 ) after that event. The visit to Nazareth recorded in Mt 13:54-58 (and Mr 6:1-6 ) we take to be not a later visit, but the same with this first one; because we cannot think that the Nazarenes, after being so enraged at His first display of wisdom as to attempt His destruction, should, on a second display of the same, wonder at it and ask how He came by it, as if they had never witnessed it before. 16. as his custom was-- Compare Ac 17:2 . stood up for to read-- Others besides rabbins were allowed to address the congregation. (See Ac 13:15 .)

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14325"/><div sID="gen27758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14325"/>18-19. To have fixed on any passage announcing His sufferings (as <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1-Isa.53.12">Is 53:1-12</reference>), would have been unsuitable at that early stage of His ministry. But He selects a passage announcing the sublime object of His whole mission, its divine character, and His special endowments for it; expressed in the first person, and so singularly adapted to the first opening of the mouth in His prophetic capacity, that it seems as if made expressly for this occasion. It is from the well-known section of Isaiah's prophecies whose burden is that mysterious "Servant of the Lord," despised of man, abhorred of the nation, but before whom kings on seeing Him are to arise, and princes to worship; in visage more marred than any man and His form than the sons of men, yet sprinkling many nations; laboring seemingly in vain, and spending His strength for naught and in vain, yet Jehovah's Servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and be His Salvation to the ends of the earth (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.1-Isa.49.26">Is 49:1-26</reference>, &c.). The quotation is chiefly from the Septuagint version, used in the synagogues. <div eID="gen27758" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14330"/><div sID="gen27765" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14330"/><hi type="bold">23. this proverb--</hi>like our "Charity begins at home."<div eID="gen27765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whatsoever, &c.--</hi>"Strange rumors have reached our ears of Thy doings at Capernaum; but if such power resides in Thee to cure the ills of humanity, why has none of it yet come nearer home, and why is all this alleged power reserved for strangers?" His choice of Capernaum as a place of residence since entering on public life was, it seems, already well known at Nazareth; and when He did come thither, to give no displays of His power when distant places were ringing with His fame, wounded their pride. He had indeed "laid his hands on a few sick folk and healed them" (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.5">Mr 6:5</reference>); but this seems to have been done quite privately the general unbelief precluding anything more open. <div eID="gen27766" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14331"/><div sID="gen27767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14331"/><hi type="bold">24. And he said, &c.--</hi>He replies to the one proverb by another, equally familiar, which we express in a rougher form--"Too much familiarity breeds contempt." Our Lord's long residence in Nazareth merely as a townsman had made Him too common, incapacitating them for appreciating Him as others did who were less familiar with His everyday demeanor in private life. A most important principle, to which the wise will pay due regard. (See also <reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Mt 7:6</reference>, on which our Lord Himself ever acted.) <div eID="gen27767" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14332"/><div sID="gen27768" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14332"/><hi type="bold">25-27. But I tell you, &c.--</hi>falling back for support on the well-known examples of Elijah and Elisha (Eliseus), whose miraculous power, passing by those who were near, expended itself on those at a distance, yea on heathens, "the two great prophets who stand at the commencement of prophetic antiquity, and whose miracles strikingly prefigured those of our Lord. As He intended like them to feed the poor and cleanse the lepers, He points to these miracles of mercy, and not to the fire from heaven and the bears that tore the mockers" [Stier].<div eID="gen27768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">three years and six months--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Jas.5.17">Jas 5:17</reference>, including perhaps the six months after the last fall of rain, when there would be little or none at any rate; whereas in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.1">1Ki 18:1</reference>, which says the rain returned "in the third year," that period is probably not reckoned. <div eID="gen27769" type="x-p"/>
